figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of multilingual brain decoding and shared cortical semantic geometry. a, SemDecoder maps neural responses to Chinese, English and French stimuli into a unified semantic space for text reconstruction. b, Illustration of different cortical response patterns and preserved relative semantic relationships across languages. Corresponding semantic contents are shown in two-dimensional representational configurations. c, Cortical maps of the principal functional gradient and shared semantic geometry gradient, with their correspondence across Schaefer-400 parcels. Surface colours indicate percentile ranks within each map. Each point in the scatter plot denotes a parcel; the black line shows a least-squares fit. The Spearman correlation and one-sided spin-test P value from 1,000 rotations are indicated. d, Zeroshot cross-language text decoding for English to Chinese, English to French and Chinese to English. BGEScore compares SemDecoder decoding with a control in which the model generates text without brain data (Random). Violin plots show participant distributions; dashed and dotted lines indicate medians and quartiles, respectively. e, Reference texts and corresponding decoded examples in English, Chinese and French. Green, yellow and red indicate exact matches, semantically similar content and unmatched content, respectively. ****P < 0.0001.

Fig. 2 Semantic decoding across languages and datasets. a, Decoding performance of SemDecoder and Tang2023 [13] across datasets. Open and filled circles indicate Tang2023 and SemDecoder, respectively; colours indicate datasets. Scores are z-normalized relative to text generated without brain data and oriented so that higher values indicate better performance; dashed line, randomized baseline. b,c, Participant-level 1 − WER (b) and BGEScore (c) across datasets and languages. n = 49, 35, 28, 6, 6 and 12 participants for LPPC-fMRI(EN), LPPC-fMRI(CN), LPPC-fMRI(FR), Chen2026(EN), Chen2026(CN) and SMN4Lang(CN), respectively. Comparisons in b,c used two-sided paired t-tests with Holm–Šidák correction across the six comparisons for each metric; asterisks indicate adjusted P values. d, Temporal BGEScore matrices comparing decoded texts with reference texts, averaged across participants. Horizontal and vertical axes indicate decoded and reference times, respectively. e, Cortical contribution to within-language semantic decoding, quantified by the decrease in brain–semantic cosine similarity after 8-mm searchlight occlusion. Colours show percentile ranks among positively contributing vertices; non-positive contributions are black. White lines mark major sulci. f, Participant-level contributions in eight temporal cortical regions, measured as the decrease in decoding performance after regional occlusion; insets identify each region. Asterisks indicate higher contributions than participants’ cortex-wide means (one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction). Dotted line, zero contribution. n = 35, 49 and 28 participants for Chinese, English and French, respectively. Boxes in b,c,f show medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs); whiskers extend to 1.5×IQR, and points beyond whiskers denote outliers. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. L, left; R, right; STS, superior temporal sulcus; TTS, transverse temporal sulcus; STG, superior temporal gyrus; PT, planum temporale; HG, Heschl’s gyrus; MTG, middle temporal gyrus. EN, English; CN, Chinese; FR, French.

Fig. 3 Cortical semantic geometry is shared across languages. a, Group-level cortical representational geometry before and after Procrustes alignment. Points denote corresponding narrative events (E1–E3), with distances reflecting dissimilarity between cortical response patterns. Similar relative configurations illustrate preserved relationships among events across languages. b, Cross-language RDM similarity between participants and the other language’s group average, pooled across both directions for each language pair. Points denote participants; dashed and dotted lines indicate medians and quartiles, respectively. c, Concreteness, socialness and arousal directions in the aligned cortical representational spaces. Arrows point from abstract to concrete, non-social to social and low to high arousal, respectively. Parallel arrows across languages indicate consistent semantic attribute directions. d, Cross-language parallelism of attribute directions versus participant-specific median random controls (n = 112 participants; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holmcorrected across three attributes). e, Correspondence of neural distances between matched event pairs across languages. Points denote event pairs; lines show least-squares fits. Spearman correlations are indicated. f, Cross-language RSA along narrative progress. Solid lines and shading show the mean and s.e.m. across windows grouped by narrative progress; dashed lines show the phase-randomized control. g, Searchlight brain–semantic RSA for each language. h, Spatial Spearman correlations between individual brain–semantic RSA maps and the group averages of the other two languages, averaged across those languages. i, Searchlight cross-language RSA for each language pair. Cyan contours in g,i outline the top 20% of mean cross-language RSA. j, Spatial Spearman correlations between individual brain–semantic and mean crosslanguage RSA maps. In h,j, n = 35, 49 and 28 participants for Chinese, English and French, respectively. Asterisks in h,j indicate correlations above participant-specific spin-null medians (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected across languages within each panel). Boxes in d,h,j show medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs); whiskers extend to 1.5×IQR, and points beyond whiskers denote outliers. ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. s.e.m., standard error of the mean; CN, Chinese; EN, English; FR, French.
